For y=x+g(c)⊙F(x), g(c)=sigmoid(Wc+b), W=0 and b=3 initialize every gate to 0.9526: context independent and close to the ungated residual baseline x+F(x), but not identical. This preserves neither an identity initialization nor exact baseline outputs; each residual contribution shrinks 4.74%. Gate placement matters: gating the shortcut also attenuates the direct gradient path, whose importance is supported by [Identity Mappings](https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.05027). Exact identity initialization instead follows from zero residual scaling, as in [ReZero](https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.04887).

Direct differentiation gives sigmoid′(3)=0.04518, versus 0.25 at bias zero: gate-logit sensitivity is about 5.5× smaller, although optimizer updates need not shrink proportionally, especially with Adam. Zero gate weights do not block their own gradients: ∂L/∂W=[(∂L/∂y)⊙F⊙g(1−g)]cᵀ, generally nonzero. They initially block gradients into a separate context encoder through the gate; shared features still receive gradients through other paths. Residual-branch gradients retain the approximately 0.953 multiplier. Thus positive bias favors baseline-like behavior while potentially delaying contextual adaptation; these are mathematical deductions, not measured NextItNet results.

Recommended controls: ungated g=1; frozen g=0.9526; learned context-independent per-layer/per-channel gates initialized identically; and a genuinely parameter-matched ungated NextItNet with additional active residual capacity. Unused dummy parameters do not control capacity. To isolate context dependence more tightly, retain the full gate network but replace its context with a fixed input. Keep training budgets, initialization of shared weights, sampling and validation identical. Adaptive gains over both static learned scaling and capacity controls support context selection; gate variance alone does not.
